title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 868–870 (Night 204, continuing nights-203), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 204 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. The eunuch tells him to be patient and not to hurry; he turns his face away and recites three lines on a beauty no words can reach. Set behind the curtain over the Lady Budūr's door, he asks whether he should cure her from there or go in to her, and the astonished eunuch says a cure from outside would be the greater credit. So he sits down behind the curtain and writes her a letter: rhymed prose on the wasting of a lover who has had no word from his beloved, verses written in tears and blood, a signature naming himself, Qamar al-Zamān son of Shahramān, and her, the Lady Budūr daughter of King al-Ghayūr, and more verses in the margin, on the cover and at the end, asking her to send back his ring for hers. He folds her own ring into the paper and gives it to the eunuch, who carries it in to his mistress, and morning overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الرَّابِعَةُ بَعْدَ الْمِائَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-rābiʿatu baʿda al-miʾatayni
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the fourth after the two-hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the two hundred and fourth night,
sentences.n: The night is numbered “the fourth after the two hundred”: al-rābiʿa, “the fourth”, is feminine to agree with layla. The ئ of المائتين is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْخَادِمَ قَالَ لِقَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ اصْبِرْ وَلَا تَسْتَعْجِلْ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-khādima qāla li-Qamari al-Zamāni iṣbir wa-lā tastaʿjil
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that the-eunuch said to-Qamar al-Zamān: Be-patient, and-do-not hurry!
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the eunuch said to Qamar al-Zamān, “Be patient, and do not be in such a hurry!”
sentences.n: Shahrazād picks up where the night before broke off, with the eunuch still running after the young man. iṣbir, imperative of ṣabara, “to be patient”: the alif is the helping one, sounded i-. lā tastaʿjil, “do not hurry”, lā with the jussive of istaʿjala, Form X.

sentences.t: فَأَعْرَضَ بِوَجْهِهِ عَنْهُ وَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: fa-aʿraḍa bi-wajhihi ʿanhu wa-anshada yaqūlu hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: And-he-turned-away with-his-face from-him and-recited saying these the-verses:
sentences.i: But he turned his face away from him and recited these verses:
sentences.n: aʿraḍa bi-wajhihi ʿan, “he turned his face away from”: bi- marks the part turned, as at the end of the night before. anshada yaqūlu, “he recited, saying”, the usual way of bringing in verse; hādhihi al-abyāta, “these verses”, is its object.

sentences.t:
اَنَا عَارِفُ بِصِفَاتِ حُسْنِكَ جَاهِلُ * مُتَحَيِّرُ لَمْ اَدْرِ مَا اَنَا قَائِلُ
لَوْ قُلْتُ شَمْسًا كَانَ حُسْنُكَ لَمْ يَغِبْ * عَنْ نَاظِرِي اِنَّ الشُّمُوسَ اَوَافِلُ
كَمُلَتْ مَحَاسِنُكَ الَّتِيْ فِيْ وَصْفِهَا * عَجَزَ الْبَلِيغُ وَحَارَ فِيْهَا الْقَائِلُ
sentences.tr:
anā ʿārifu bi-ṣifāti ḥusnika jāhilu * mutaḥayyiru lam adri mā anā qāʾilu
law qultu shamsan kāna ḥusnuka lam yaghib * ʿan nāẓirī inna al-shumūsa awāfilu
kamulat maḥāsinuka allatī fī waṣfihā * ʿajaza al-balīghu wa-ḥāra fīhā al-qāʾilu
sentences.l:
I, knowing (the) qualities (of) your-beauty, (am) ignorant, * bewildered; not I-know what I (am) saying.
If I-said a-sun, was your-beauty not setting * from my-eye; indeed the-suns (are) setting-ones.
Perfect-became your-charms, which in describing-them * fell-short the-eloquent, and-was-at-a-loss in-them the-speaker.
sentences.i:
I know the marks of your beauty, and yet I know nothing; * bewildered, I cannot tell what I should say.
Were I to call you a sun — but your beauty never sets * from my sight, and suns go down.
Your charms are perfect: to describe them the eloquent fall short, * and the speaker stands lost before them.
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed. The rhyme falls on jāhilu / awāfilu / al-qāʾilu. The first line turns on a paradox: ʿārif bi-, “knowing”, and jāhil, “ignorant”, of the same beauty — he knows its features but has no words for them; bi- marks what is known. The print sets a single ḍamma on عَارِفُ and مُتَحَيِّرُ, where the metre wants tanwīn, ʿārifun and mutaḥayyirun; the print's pointing is kept. lam adri, “I do not know”: the jussive of darā, which loses its final yāʾ. mā anā qāʾilu, “what I am to say”. In the second line law qultu shamsan, “if I said ‘a sun’”, breaks off: a sun will not do, for the sun sets and her beauty never leaves his sight. lam yaghib ʿan, “did not set, vanish from”. awāfil, plural of āfil, “setting”, said of stars. kamula, “to be complete, perfect”. maḥāsin, “charms, beauties”, a plural with no singular in use. allatī fī waṣfihā ʿajaza …, “which in describing them the eloquent fell short”: the relative clause is fronted on its fī, and -hā returns to maḥāsin. ʿajaza, “to be unable”; ḥāra fī, “to be at a loss over”. The print sets a sukūn on the long yāʾ of الَّتِيْ, فِيْ and فِيْهَا, as it often does.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْخَادِمَ أَوْقَفَ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ خَلْفَ السِّتَارَةِ الَّتِي عَلَي الْبَابِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-khādima awqafa Qamara al-Zamāni khalfa al-sitārati allatī ʿalā al-bābi
sentences.l: Then indeed the-eunuch made-stand Qamar al-Zamān behind the-curtain which (was) on the-door.
sentences.i: Then the eunuch stood Qamar al-Zamān behind the curtain that hung over the door.
sentences.n: thumma inna …, “then …”: inna only opens the new step of the story. awqafa, Form IV of waqafa, “to make stand, halt”. sitāra, “curtain”. The print spells ʿalā as علي, with ي, instead of على; it is kept and read ʿalā.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ أَيُّ الْحَالَتَيْنِ أَحَبُّ إِلَيْكَ أَكُونُ أُدَاوِي سَيِّدَتَكَ وَأُبْرِؤُهَا مِنْ هُنَا أَوْ أَدْخُلُ إِلَيْهَا فَأُبْرِؤُهَا مِنْ دَاخِلِ السِّتَارَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Qamaru al-Zamāni ayyu al-ḥālatayni aḥabbu ilayka akūnu udāwī sayyidataka wa-ubriʾuhā min hunā aw adkhulu ilayhā fa-ubriʾuhā min dākhili al-sitārati
sentences.l: And-said to-him Qamar al-Zamān: Which (of) the-two-ways (is) dearer to-you: I-be treating your-lady and-curing-her from here, or I-go-in to-her and-cure-her from inside the-curtain?
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān said to him, “Which would you like better — that I treat your lady and cure her from here, or that I go in to her and cure her inside the curtain?”
sentences.n: ayyu al-ḥālatayni, “which of the two states”: ayy before a definite dual asks “which of the two”. aḥabbu ilayka, “dearer to you”, the elative of ḥabīb; ilā marks the one to whom a thing is dear. akūnu udāwī, “I am to be treating”, kāna with the imperfect for an ongoing act; the two choices stand side by side without an, as in speech. dāwā, Form III, “to treat (a patient)”. abraʾa, Form IV, “to cure”: the print writes its hamza on wāw, ابرؤها, twice, where Classical spelling puts it on yāʾ after the kasra, ابرئها; the seat follows the vowel after the hamza, a common later spelling, and it is kept. min dākhili, “from the inside of”. The shaddas of ايّ and سيّدتك are printed.

sentences.t: فَتَعَجَّبَ الْخَادِمُ مِنْ كَلَامِهِ وَقَالَ لَهُ إِنْ أَبْرَأْتَهَا مِنْ هُنَا كَانَ ذٰلِكَ زِيَادَةً فِي فَضْلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-taʿajjaba al-khādimu min kalāmihi wa-qāla lahu in abraʾtahā min hunā kāna dhālika ziyādatan fī faḍlika
sentences.l: And-wondered the-eunuch at his-speech and-said to-him: If you-cured-her from here, would-be that an-increase in your-merit.
sentences.i: The eunuch was astonished at his words and said to him, “If you cure her from here, that will add all the more to your credit.”
sentences.n: taʿajjaba min, Form V, “to wonder at”: min marks what causes the wonder. in abraʾtahā …, kāna …, “if you cure her …, it will be …”: after in both verbs are perfect with a future sense. ziyādatan fī faḍlika, “an increase in your excellence”. The hamza of ابرأتها is printed.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذٰلِكَ جَلَسَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ خَلْفَ السِّتَارَةِ وَأَخْرَجَ الدَّوَاةَ وَالْقَلَمَ وَأَخَذَ وَرَقَةً وَكَتَبَ فِيهَا هٰذِهِ الْكَلِمَاتِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika jalasa Qamaru al-Zamāni khalfa al-sitārati wa-akhraja al-dawāta wa-al-qalama wa-akhadha waraqatan wa-kataba fīhā hādhihi al-kalimāti
sentences.l: And-at that sat Qamar al-Zamān behind the-curtain, and-brought-out the-inkpot and-the-pen, and-took a-sheet and-wrote on-it these the-words:
sentences.i: Thereupon Qamar al-Zamān sat down behind the curtain, took out inkpot and pen, and taking a sheet of paper, wrote on it these words:
sentences.n: fa-ʿinda dhālika, “at that”, “thereupon”. dawāt, “inkpot”, the scribe's kit he carries as an astrologer. waraqa, “a leaf, sheet of paper”. What follows is rhymed prose, sajʿ, with the print's own asterisk between the clauses.

sentences.t: هٰذَا كِتَابُ مَنْ بَرَّحَ بِهِ الْجَوَى * وَأَتْلَفَهُ الْهَوَى * وَأَهْلَكَهُ الْأَسَى *
sentences.tr: hādhā kitābu man barraḥa bihi al-jawā * wa-atlafahu al-hawā * wa-ahlakahu al-asā *
sentences.l: This (is the) letter (of) one-whom tormented him the-passion, * and-wasted-him the-love, * and-destroyed-him the-grief. *
sentences.i: This is the letter of one whom passion has tormented, * whom love has wasted, * whom grief has destroyed;
sentences.n: The letter opens in sajʿ, rhymed prose: each clause ends on the same sound, here -ā, al-jawā / al-hawā / al-asā. kitābu man …, “the letter of one who …”: man is “one whom”, and -hi and -hu return to him. barraḥa bi-, Form II, “to torment, distress sorely”: bi- marks the one tormented. jawā, “inward burning, passion”; hawā, “love, desire”; asā, “grief”: all three are spelt with ى. atlafa, Form IV, “to waste, ruin”; ahlaka, Form IV, “to destroy”. The ḍamma of كتابُ and the fatḥa of مَن are printed.

sentences.t: وَالْبَلَاءُ لِمَنْ يَئِسَ مِنَ الْحَيَاةِ * وَأَيْقَنَ بِحُلُولِ الْوَفَاةِ *
sentences.tr: wa-al-balāʾu li-man yaʾisa mina al-ḥayāti * wa-ayqana bi-ḥulūli al-wafāti *
sentences.l: And-the-affliction (is) for-one-who has-despaired of the-life * and-been-certain of-(the)-arrival (of) the-death. *
sentences.i: affliction is the lot of one who has despaired of life * and is sure that death is at hand.
sentences.n: The rhyme moves to -āh, al-ḥayāh / al-wafāh, the endings dropped in pause. wa-al-balāʾu li-man …, “and affliction belongs to one who …”, a loose nominal clause in the run of the sajʿ; it may also be read with what goes before, “whom grief and affliction have destroyed”, though the print's asterisk falls after al-asā. li- marks the one affliction belongs to. yaʾisa min, “to despair of”: min marks what is given up. ayqana bi-, Form IV, “to be certain of”: the verb takes bi- for what one is sure of. ḥulūl, “alighting, arrival”; wafāt, “death”. The ئ of يئس is printed.

sentences.t: وَمَا لِقَلْبِهِ الْحَزِينِ * مِنْ مُسْعِفٍ وَلَا مُعِينٍ * وَمَا لِطَرْفِهِ السَّاهِرِ * عَلَى الْهَمِّ نَاصِرٌ *
sentences.tr: wa-mā li-qalbihi al-ḥazīni * min musʿifin wa-lā muʿīnin * wa-mā li-ṭarfihi al-sāhiri * ʿalā al-hammi nāṣirun *
sentences.l: And-not (is there) for-his-heart the-sad * of a-succourer nor a-helper, * and-not (is there) for-his-eye the-wakeful * against the-care a-supporter. *
sentences.i: His sorrowing heart has none to succour it, * none to help; * his wakeful eye has none * to stand by it against its cares.
sentences.n: Two rhymes in pairs: al-ḥazīn / muʿīn, al-sāhir / nāṣir. mā li-X min Y, “X has no Y at all”: li- marks the one who has, and min before the indefinite noun means “any”. musʿif, “one who comes to the rescue”, active participle of Form IV asʿafa. ṭarf, “eye, glance”. sāhir, “wakeful, sleepless”. ʿalā al-hammi nāṣirun, “a helper against care”: ʿalā marks what one is helped against; here nāṣir is nominative, the subject of the second mā li- clause without min.

sentences.t: فَنَهَارُهُ فِي لَهِيبٍ * وَلَيْلُهُ فِي تَعْذِيبٍ * وَقَدِ انْبَرَى جِسْمُهُ مِنْ كَثْرَةِ النُّحُولِ * وَلَمْ يَأْتِهِ مِنْ حَبِيبِهِ رَسُولٌ *
sentences.tr: fa-nahāruhu fī lahībin * wa-layluhu fī taʿdhībin * wa-qadi inbarā jismuhu min kathrati al-nuḥūli * wa-lam yaʾtihi min ḥabībihi rasūlun *
sentences.l: So-his-day (is) in a-blaze, * and-his-night in torment; * and-has been-pared-thin his-body from (the) abundance (of) the-wasting, * and-not came-to-him from his-beloved a-messenger. *
sentences.i: His days are spent in flame, * his nights in torment; * his body is worn thin with wasting, * and no messenger has come to him from his beloved.
sentences.n: Rhymes lahīb / taʿdhīb, al-nuḥūl / rasūl. lahīb, “flame, blaze”. inbarā, Form VII of barā, “to pare (a reed pen)”, so “to be pared away, worn thin”; after qad it takes a helping kasra, qadi inbarā. nuḥūl, “emaciation, wasting”. lam yaʾtihi, “did not come to him”: the jussive of atā, which drops its final yāʾ; the hamza of يأته is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ كَتَبَ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: thumma kataba hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: Then he-wrote these the-verses:
sentences.i: Then he wrote these verses:

sentences.t:
كَتَبْتُ وَلِي قَلْبٌ بِذِكْرِكِ مُوْلَعُ * وَجَفْنٌ قَرِيحٌ مِنْ دِمَائِي يَدْمَعُ
وَجِسْمٌ كَسَاهُ لَاعِجُ الشَّوْقِ وَالْاَسَى * قَمِيصَ نُحُولٍ فَهُوَ فِيهِ مُضَعْضَعُ
شَكَوْتُ الْهَوَي لَمَّا اَضَرَّ بِي الْهَوَى * وَلَمْ يَبْقَ عِنْدِي لِلتَّصَبُّرِ مَوْضِعُ
اِلَيْكِ فَجُودِي وَارْحَمِي وَتَعَطَّفِي * فَاِنَّ فُؤَادِي بِالْهَوَى يَتَقَطَّعُ
sentences.tr:
katabtu wa-lī qalbun bi-dhikriki mūlaʿu * wa-jafnun qarīḥun min dimāʾī yadmaʿu
wa-jismun kasāhu lāʿiju al-shawqi wa-al-asā * qamīṣa nuḥūlin fa-huwa fīhi muḍaʿḍaʿu
shakawtu al-hawā lammā aḍarra bī al-hawā * wa-lam yabqa ʿindī li-al-taṣabburi mawḍiʿu
ilayki fa-jūdī wa-irḥamī wa-taʿaṭṭafī * fa-inna fuʾādī bi-al-hawā yataqaṭṭaʿu
sentences.l:
I-wrote, and-to-me (is) a-heart with-remembrance-of-you enamoured, * and-an-eyelid ulcered, from my-blood shedding-tears;
and-a-body clothed-it (the) burning (of) the-longing and-the-grief * (in the) shirt (of) wasting, so-it in-it (is) shaken.
I-complained-of the-love when harmed me the-love, * and-not remained with-me for-the-patience a-place —
to-you! So-be-generous, and-have-mercy, and-be-kind, * for-indeed my-heart by-the-love is-being-cut-to-pieces.
sentences.i:
I write with a heart that is mad for the thought of you, * and an eyelid sore with weeping, that weeps my blood,
and a body that the burn of longing and grief * has clad in a shirt of wasting, and it trembles within it.
I made my plaint of love when love had done me harm, * and in me no room was left for bearing it —
my plaint to you: be generous, have mercy, show me kindness, * for my heart by love is cut to pieces.
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed. The rhyme falls on mūlaʿu / yadmaʿu / muḍaʿḍaʿu / mawḍiʿu / yataqaṭṭaʿu. The -ki of bi-dhikriki and ilayki is feminine: he writes to the princess. katabtu wa-lī qalbun …, “I wrote, having a heart …”, a clause of state with wa-; li- marks the one who has. bi-dhikriki mūlaʿ, “enamoured of the mention of you”: awlaʿa bi-, “to make passionately fond of”, takes bi- for the object of the passion. jafn qarīḥ, “an ulcered eyelid”, from long weeping; min dimāʾī yadmaʿu, “weeps with my blood”, min marking what it sheds. kasāhu … qamīṣa nuḥūlin, “clothed it in a shirt of wasting”: kasā takes two objects. lāʿij, “burning, consuming”, said of love. muḍaʿḍaʿ, “shaken, enfeebled”, passive participle of ḍaʿḍaʿa. In the third line the print spells the first al-hawā as الْهَوَي, with ي, and the second as الْهَوَى; both are kept. aḍarra bi-, Form IV, “to harm”: the verb takes bi- for the one harmed, here bī, “me”, its long ī shortened in sound before the article. taṣabbur, Form V, “forcing oneself to be patient”, with li-: “room for patience”. The sense runs over the line-end: shakawtu al-hawā … ilayki, “I complained of love … to you”, ilā marking the one complained to. jūdī, irḥamī, taʿaṭṭafī, three feminine imperatives. bi-al-hawā, “by love”: bi- marks the cause. The print sets a sukūn on the wāw of مُوْلَعُ, as it often does on a long vowel.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ كَتَبَ تَحْتَ الشِّعْرِ هٰذِهِ السَّجَعَاتِ
sentences.tr: thumma kataba taḥta al-shiʿri hādhihi al-sajaʿāti
sentences.l: Then he-wrote under the-verse these the-rhymed-phrases:
sentences.i: Then beneath the verses he wrote these rhymed lines:
sentences.n: sajaʿāt, plural of sajʿa, “a rhymed phrase”, the unit of sajʿ.

sentences.t: شِفَاءُ الْقُلُوبِ * لِقَاءُ الْمَحْبُوبِ * مَنْ جَفَاهُ حَبِيبُهُ * فَاللّٰهُ طَبِيبُهُ *
sentences.tr: shifāʾu al-qulūbi * liqāʾu al-maḥbūbi * man jafāhu ḥabībuhu * fa-Allāhu ṭabībuhu *
sentences.l: (The) cure (of) the-hearts * (is the) meeting (of) the-beloved. * Whoever shunned-him his-beloved, * then-God (is) his-physician. *
sentences.i: The cure of hearts * is meeting the beloved; * whom his beloved shuns, * God is his physician.
sentences.n: Two rhyming pairs, al-qulūb / al-maḥbūb and ḥabībuhu / ṭabībuhu. The first is a nominal sentence of two definite terms: “the cure of hearts is the meeting of the beloved”. man jafāhu …, fa-…: man, “whoever”, opens a condition, and fa- brings in the answer. jafā, “to treat harshly, shun”. ṭabīb, “physician”: fitting, from a man posing as a healer.

sentences.t: مَنْ خَانَ مِنْكُمْ وَمِنَّا * لَا نَالَ مَايَتَمَنَّى *
sentences.tr: man khāna minkum wa-minnā * lā nāla mā yatamannā *
sentences.l: Whoever betrayed of-you and-of-us, * may-not he-attain what-he-wishes. *
sentences.i: Whoever of you or of us proves false, * may he never gain what he longs for!
sentences.n: Rhyme minnā / yatamannā. khāna, “to betray, break faith”. min marks the group someone belongs to: minkum, “of you”, with the plural of politeness. lā nāla, “may he not attain”: lā with the perfect makes a wish, here a curse. tamannā, Form V, “to wish for”. The print runs mā and yatamannā together, مايتمنّى; it is kept as set. The shaddas of ومنّا and مايتمنّى are printed.

sentences.t: وَلَا أَظْرَفَ مِنَ الْمُحِبِّ الْوَافِي * إِلَي الْحَبِيبِ الْجَافِي *
sentences.tr: wa-lā aẓrafa mina al-muḥibbi al-wāfī * ilā al-ḥabībi al-jāfī *
sentences.l: And-no more-graceful (is there) than the-lover the-faithful * to the-beloved the-harsh. *
sentences.i: And none is more gracious than the lover who keeps faith * with a beloved who is cruel.
sentences.n: Rhyme al-wāfī / al-jāfī. The sense of this clause is not certain. As printed, wa-lā aẓrafa min …, “there is none more graceful than …”, with the lā that denies a whole kind, followed by the noun in the accusative without tanwīn; aẓraf is the elative of ẓarīf, “elegant, graceful, refined”. That reading is kept and pointed here, but a slip for another elative, such as aẓlam, “more wronged”, cannot be ruled out. al-wāfī, “faithful, keeping one's word”; al-jāfī, “harsh, one who shuns”, active participles of wafā and jafā. The print spells ilā as الي, with ي, instead of الى; it is kept and read ilā. ilā marks the one he keeps faith towards.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ كَتَبَ فِى الْإِمْضَاءِ مِنَ الْهَائِمِ الْوَلْهَانِ * الْعَاشِقِ الْحَيْرَانِ * مَنْ أَقْلَقَهُ الْعِشْقُ وَالْغَرَامُ * أَسِيرِ الْوَجَلِ وَالْهَيَامِ * قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ * ابْنِ شَهْرَمَانَ *
sentences.tr: thumma kataba fī al-imḍāʾi mina al-hāʾimi al-walhāni * al-ʿāshiqi al-ḥayrāni * man aqlaqahu al-ʿishqu wa-al-gharāmu * asīri al-wajali wa-al-hayāmi * Qamari al-Zamāni * ibni Shahramāna *
sentences.l: Then he-wrote in the-signature: From the-wanderer the-distraught, * the-lover the-bewildered, * one-whom disquieted-him the-passion and-the-ardour, * (the) captive (of) the-fear and-the-love-madness, * Qamar al-Zamān, * son (of) Shahramān, *
sentences.i: Then he signed it: From the love-crazed, distracted wanderer, * the bewildered lover, * the man whom passion and longing give no rest, * the captive of fear and love-madness, * Qamar al-Zamān, * son of Shahramān,
sentences.n: imḍāʾ, “signature”, the closing of the letter, which names sender and addressee in sajʿ, the rhymes running al-walhān / al-ḥayrān / Shahramān and al-gharām / al-hayām. The print spells fī as فى, with ى, as it often does. hāʾim, “one wandering distraught with love”; walhān and ḥayrān, “distraught”, “bewildered”, adjectives on the faʿlān pattern. min marks the sender. The epithets that follow are all genitive in apposition to al-hāʾim, after min; man aqlaqahu …, “one whom … disquieted”, stands in their place. aqlaqa, Form IV, “to disquiet, give no rest”. ʿishq and gharām, two words for passionate love; wajal, “fear”; hayām, “love-madness”. ibn is written with its alif here, ابن, and Shahramān is diptote, -a in the genitive. The fatḥa of مَن is printed.

sentences.t: إِلَى فَرِيدَةِ الزَّمَانِ * وَنُخْبَةِ الْحُورِ الْحِسَانِ * السَّيِّدَةِ بُدُورَ * بِنْتِ الْمَلِكِ الْغَيُورِ *
sentences.tr: ilā farīdati al-zamāni * wa-nukhbati al-ḥūri al-ḥisāni * al-sayyidati Budūra * binti al-maliki al-Ghayūri *
sentences.l: To (the) unique-one (of) the-age, * and-(the)-choicest (of) the-houris the-beautiful, * the-Lady Budūr, * daughter (of) the-King al-Ghayūr. *
sentences.i: To the pearl of her age, * the choicest of the fair houris, * the Lady Budūr, * daughter of King al-Ghayūr:
sentences.n: ilā marks the one the letter goes to. The rhymes are al-zamān / al-ḥisān and Budūr / al-Ghayūr. farīda, “a unique pearl”, and so “the one without peer”; farīdatu al-zamāni, “the unique one of the age”, plays on the sender's own name, Qamar al-Zamān. nukhba, “the choice, the pick”. ḥūr, “houris”, the dark-eyed maidens of Paradise; ḥisān, “beautiful”, plural of ḥasana. Budūr is diptote, -a in the genitive.

sentences.t: اعْلَمِي أَنَّنِي فِي لَيْلِي سَهْرَانُ * وَفِي نَهَارِي حَيْرَانُ * زَائِدَ النُّحُولِ وَالْأَسْقَامِ * وَالْعِشْقِ وَالْغَرَامِ *
sentences.tr: iʿlamī annanī fī laylī sahrānu * wa-fī nahārī ḥayrānu * zāʾida al-nuḥūli wa-al-asqāmi * wa-al-ʿishqi wa-al-gharāmi *
sentences.l: Know that-I in my-night (am) wakeful * and-in my-day bewildered, * exceeding (in) the-wasting and-the-sicknesses * and-the-passion and-the-ardour. *
sentences.i: Know that by night I lie sleepless * and by day I wander bewildered, * ever more wasted and sick, * ever deeper in passion and longing;
sentences.n: iʿlamī, “know!”, feminine imperative of ʿalima; the alif is the helping one. annanī, “that I”, with the -nī of anna. sahrān, “sleepless”, ḥayrān, “bewildered”, are predicates of anna, nominative; as faʿlān adjectives they take no tanwīn. zāʾida al-nuḥūli …, “abounding in wasting …”, is read here as a circumstantial accusative, like kathīra and ghazīra below: zāʾid, “increasing”, in construct with what increases. asqām, plural of saqam, “sickness”. The rhymes are sahrān / ḥayrān and al-asqām / al-gharām. The shadda of انّني is printed.

sentences.t: كَثِيرَ الزَّفَرَاتِ * غَزِيرَ الْعَبَرَاتِ * أَسِيرُ الْهَوَى * قَتِيلُ الْجَوَى * وَالْهَجْرُ لِقَلْبِهِ كَوَى * غَرِيمُ الْغَرَامِ * نَدِيمُ السَّقَامِ *
sentences.tr: kathīra al-zafarāti * ghazīra al-ʿabarāti * asīru al-hawā * qatīlu al-jawā * wa-al-hajru li-qalbihi kawā * gharīmu al-gharāmi * nadīmu al-saqāmi *
sentences.l: Many (in) the-sighs, * abundant (in) the-tears; * captive (of) the-love, * slain (of) the-passion, * and-the-separation his-heart seared; * debtor (of) the-ardour, * boon-companion (of) the-sickness. *
sentences.i: my sighs are many, * my tears abundant; * I am love's captive, * slain by passion, * one whose heart separation has seared, * held in thrall by longing, * sickness my boon companion.
sentences.n: The print has كثيرا لزفرات, a misprint for كثير الزفرات, corrected here: the alif of the article was set on the end of the word before. The print has فزير, a misprint for غزير, corrected here. kathīra al-zafarāti, ghazīra al-ʿabarāti, “many of sighs, abundant of tears”: adjectives in construct with what they describe, accusative as circumstantial terms like zāʾida above. The rhymes run al-zafarāt / al-ʿabarāt, al-hawā / al-jawā / kawā, al-gharām / al-saqām. asīru al-hawā and the epithets after it are nominative, further predicates of “I”. In wa-al-hajru li-qalbihi kawā, “and separation has seared his heart”, the letter slips into the third person; kawā, “to brand, cauterise”, and li- marks its object, put before the verb. gharīm, “creditor, debtor, one bound to another”, plays on gharām, “ardour”: he is pursued by longing as by a creditor. nadīm, “drinking companion”.

sentences.t: فَأَنَا السَّهْرَانُ الَّذِي لَا تَهْجَعُ مُقْلَتُهُ * وَالْمُتَيَّمُ الَّذِي لَا تَرْقَأُ عَبْرَتُهُ * فَنَارُ قَلْبِي لَا تَطْفَى * وَلَهِيبُ شَوْقِي لَا يَخْفَى *
sentences.tr: fa-anā al-sahrānu alladhī lā tahjaʿu muqlatuhu * wa-al-mutayyamu alladhī lā tarqaʾu ʿabratuhu * fa-nāru qalbī lā taṭfā * wa-lahību shawqī lā yakhfā *
sentences.l: So-I (am) the-wakeful-one who not sleeps his-eye, * and-the-enslaved-one who not dries his-tear; * so-(the)-fire (of) my-heart not is-quenched, * and-(the)-flame (of) my-longing not is-hidden. *
sentences.i: I am the sleepless one whose eye never closes, * the love-enslaved whose tears never dry; * the fire in my heart is never quenched, * and the flame of my longing cannot be hidden.
sentences.n: Rhymes muqlatuhu / ʿabratuhu and taṭfā / yakhfā. alladhī lā tahjaʿu muqlatuhu, “who — his eye does not sleep”: the -hu of muqlatuhu returns to alladhī. hajaʿa, “to sleep (at night)”; muqla, “eye, eyeball”. mutayyam, “enslaved by love”, passive participle of tayyama. raqaʾa, “to stop flowing”, of tears; the hamza of ترقأ is printed. ʿabra, “a tear”. lā taṭfā, “is not quenched”: Classical ṭafiʾa, yaṭfaʾu, has a hamza; the print writes تطفى without it, as speech does, and so it rhymes with yakhfā. nār, “fire”, is feminine. The shadda of المتيّم is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ كَتَبَ فِي حَاشِيَةِ الْكِتَابِ هٰذَا الْبَيْتَ الْمُسْتَطَابَ شِعْرٌ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Qamara al-Zamāni kataba fī ḥāshiyati al-kitābi hādhā al-bayta al-mustaṭāba shiʿrun
sentences.l: Then indeed Qamar al-Zamān wrote in (the) margin (of) the-letter this the-verse the-delightful. Verse:
sentences.i: Then Qamar al-Zamān wrote in the margin of the letter this charming line:
sentences.n: ḥāshiya, “margin, edge”. mustaṭāb, “found sweet, delightful”, passive participle of Form X istaṭāba. The last word, shiʿr, “verse”, is the print's own heading for the line that follows, not part of the sentence.

sentences.t: سَلَامُ مِنْ خَزَائِنِ لُطْفِ رَبِّي * عَلَى مَنْ عِنْدَهَا رُوْحِي وَقَلْبِي
sentences.tr: salāmu min khazāʾini luṭfi rabbī * ʿalā man ʿindahā rūḥī wa-qalbī
sentences.l: Greeting from (the) treasuries (of the) kindness (of) my-Lord * upon (her) whom with-her (are) my-soul and-my-heart.
sentences.i: Greetings from the treasuries of my Lord's kindness * upon her who holds my soul and my heart.
sentences.n: The verse is pointed in the print and copied as printed. The rhyme falls on rabbī / qalbī. salām … ʿalā, “greeting … upon”, the formula of greeting; ʿalā marks the one greeted. The print sets a single ḍamma on سَلَامُ, where the metre wants tanwīn, salāmun; the print's pointing is kept. min marks where the greeting comes from. khazāʾin, plural of khizāna, “treasury”. man ʿindahā, “one with whom are”: ʿinda marks what she holds, and the -hā shows that man is a woman. The print sets a sukūn on the wāw of رُوْحِي.

sentences.t: وَكَتَبَ أَيْضًا
sentences.tr: wa-kataba ayḍan
sentences.l: And-he-wrote also:
sentences.i: He also wrote:

sentences.t:
هَبُوا لِي حَدِيثًا مِنْ حَدِيثِكُمْ عَسَى * بِهِ تَرْحَمُونِي اَوْ يَقِرُّ جَنَانِي
وَمِنْ شَغَفِي فِيكُمْ وَوَجْدِي اِنَّنِي * اُهَوِّنُ مَا اَلْقَاهُ وَهُوَ هَوَانِي
رَعَى اللّٰهُ قَوْمًا شَطَّ عَنِّي مَزَارُهُمْ * كَتَمْتُ هَوَاهُمْ فِي اَعَزِّ مَكَانِ
وَهَا اَنَا قَدْ جَادَ الزَّمَانُ بِفَضْلِهِ * وَفِي تُرْبِ اَعْتَابِ الْحَبِيبِ رَمَانِي
رَأَيْتُ بُدُورًا فِي الْفِرَاشِ بِجَانِبِي * زَهَا قَمَرِي مِنْ شَمْسِهَا بِزَمَانِي
sentences.tr:
habū lī ḥadīthan min ḥadīthikum ʿasā * bihi tarḥamūnī aw yaqirru janānī
wa-min shaghafī fīkum wa-wajdī innanī * uhawwinu mā alqāhu wa-huwa hawānī
raʿā Allāhu qawman shaṭṭa ʿannī mazāruhum * katamtu hawāhum fī aʿazzi makāni
wa-hā anā qad jāda al-zamānu bi-faḍlihi * wa-fī turbi aʿtābi al-ḥabībi ramānī
raʾaytu budūran fī al-firāshi bi-jānibī * zahā qamarī min shamsihā bi-zamānī
sentences.l:
Grant to-me a-word from your-talk; perhaps * by-it you-will-pity-me or will-be-at-rest my-heart.
And-from my-passion for-you and-my-longing, indeed-I * make-light-of what I-meet, and-it (is) my-abasement.
May-guard God a-people far-is from-me their-visiting-place; * I-hid love-of-them in (the) dearest place.
And-here I (am): has been-generous the-Time with-its-bounty, * and-into (the) dust (of the) thresholds (of) the-beloved it-has-cast-me.
I-saw full-moons in the-bed at-my-side; * shone my-moon from her-sun in-my-time.
sentences.i:
Grant me some word of your speech, that through it * you may take pity on me, or my heart find rest.
So deep is my passion and longing for you * that I make light of all I suffer, though it brings me low.
God keep a people whose dwelling is far from me! * I have hidden my love for them in the dearest place.
And now Time has been generous with its bounty * and cast me down in the dust of my beloved's thresholds.
I saw full moons upon the bed beside me; * my moon grew bright from her sun in my own time.
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed. The rhyme falls on janānī / hawānī / makāni / ramānī / bi-zamānī. habū, “grant!”, plural imperative of wahaba; the plural -kum, “you”, is the polite plural for the beloved. ʿasā bihi tarḥamūnī, “perhaps by it you will pity me”: bi- marks the means, the word she sends. qarra, “to be still, at rest”; janān, “heart”. min shaghafī fīkum, “from my passion for you”: min gives the cause, and fī marks the one loved. hawwana, Form II, “to make light of”; the line plays hawā, “love”, against hawān, “abasement”. raʿā Allāhu, “may God guard”: the perfect makes a wish. shaṭṭa ʿan, “to be far from”; mazār, “place visited”. aʿazzu makānin, “the dearest place”, his heart; makāni without tanwīn for the rhyme. jāda bi-, “to be generous with”: bi- marks what is given. turb, “dust”; aʿtāb, plural of ʿataba, “threshold”. The last line puns on all three names: budūr, “full moons”, is the princess Budūr; qamarī, “my moon”, is Qamar al-Zamān himself; and zamānī, “my time”, echoes al-Zamān. He recalls the night he found her in his bed. zahā, “to shine, be bright”. bi-jānibī, “at my side”, and bi-zamānī, “in my time”: bi- marks place and time.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ بَعْدَ أَنْ خَتَمَ الْكِتَابَ كَتَبَ فِي عُنْوَانِهِ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Qamara al-Zamāni baʿda an khatama al-kitāba kataba fī ʿunwānihi hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: Then indeed Qamar al-Zamān, after that he-sealed the-letter, wrote on its-address these the-verses:
sentences.i: Then, when he had sealed the letter, Qamar al-Zamān wrote these verses on the outside where the address goes:
sentences.n: baʿda an khatama, “after he had sealed”: an with the perfect makes a clause that baʿda governs. khatama, “to seal”. ʿunwān, the superscription or address written on the outside of a folded letter.

sentences.t:
سَلِي كِتَابِي عَمَّا خَطَّهُ قَلَمِي * فَالرَّسْمُ يُخْبِرُ عَنْ وَجْدِي وَعَنْ اَلَمِي
يَدِي تَخُطُّ وَدَمْعُ الْعَيْنِ مُنْهَمِلٌ * وَقَدْ شَكَى الشَّوْقَ لِلْقِرْطَاسِ مِنْ قَلَمِي
مَازَالَ دَمْعِي عَلَى الْقِرْطَاسِ مُنْسَكِبًا * اِنِ انْقَضَتْ اَدْمُعِي اَتْبَعْتُهَا بِدَمِي
sentences.tr:
salī kitābī ʿammā khaṭṭahu qalamī * fa-al-rasmu yukhbiru ʿan wajdī wa-ʿan alamī
yadī takhuṭṭu wa-damʿu al-ʿayni munhamilun * wa-qad shakā al-shawqa li-al-qirṭāsi min qalamī
mā zāla damʿī ʿalā al-qirṭāsi munsakiban * ini inqaḍat admuʿī atbaʿtuhā bi-damī
sentences.l:
Ask my-letter about-what traced-it my-pen; * for-the-writing tells of my-longing and-of my-pain.
My-hand traces, and-(the)-tear (of) the-eye (is) pouring, * and-it-has complained-of the-longing to-the-paper from my-pen.
Not ceased my-tear on the-paper pouring; * if ran-out my-tears, I-made-follow-them with-my-blood.
sentences.i:
Ask my letter what my pen has traced: * its lines tell of my longing and my pain.
My hand writes on while the tears stream from my eyes, * and through my pen they have poured their plaint of longing on the page.
My tears flow on the paper still; * should my tears run dry, I will follow them with my blood.
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed. The rhyme falls on qalamī / alamī / qalamī / bi-damī. salī, feminine imperative of saʾala, “ask!”, in the short form without hamza; ʿammā is ʿan mā, “about what”. rasm, “trace, writing”. akhbara ʿan, “to tell of”: ʿan marks what the news is about. wa-damʿu al-ʿayni munhamilun, “while the eye's tear pours”, a clause of state with wa-. In wa-qad shakā al-shawqa li-al-qirṭāsi min qalamī the subject of shakā, “complained of”, is not named; it is most likely the tear, which tells its longing to the paper by way of the pen, li- marking the one complained to and min the way it comes; the print spells shakā with ى. qirṭās, “paper, sheet”. mā zāla … munsakiban, “has not ceased pouring”. ini inqaḍat …, atbaʿtuhā …, “if they run out, I will make them follow …”: both verbs are perfect with a future sense after in; atbaʿa, Form IV, “to make follow”; bi- marks what follows, “with my blood”. The print joins mā and zāla, مَازَالَ.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ كَتَبَ أَيْضًا فِي آخِرِ الْكِتَابِ
sentences.tr: thumma kataba ayḍan fī ākhiri al-kitābi
sentences.l: Then he-wrote also at (the) end (of) the-letter:
sentences.i: Then at the end of the letter he also wrote:
sentences.n: The madda of آخر is printed.

sentences.t: اَرْسَلْتُ خَاتَمَكَ الَّذِي اسْتَبْدَلْتُهُ * يَوْمَ التَّوَاصُلِ فَارْسِلِي لِي خَاتَمِي
sentences.tr: arsaltu khātamaka alladhī istabdaltuhu * yawma al-tawāṣuli fa-irsilī lī khātamī
sentences.l: I-have-sent your-ring which I-took-in-exchange-for-it * (on the) day (of) the-union; so-send to-me my-ring!
sentences.i: I send you your ring, which I took in exchange * on the day we were together: now send me back my ring.
sentences.n: The verse is pointed in the print and copied as printed. istabdala, Form X, “to take in exchange”: he recalls the night when he and Budūr exchanged rings while she slept. tawāṣul, “union, meeting of lovers”, Form VI. The beloved is addressed with masculine -ka in khātamaka, “your ring”, as love poetry often speaks of her, though the imperative fa-rsilī is feminine. The print points fa-rsilī without the hamza of Form IV arsala, as the metre wants; Classical spelling is fa-arsilī. li- in lī marks the one the ring is sent to.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ جَعَلَ خَاتَمَ السِّتِّ بُدُورَ فِى طَيِّ الْوَرَقَةِ وَنَاوَلَهَا لِلْخَادِمِ فَأَخَذَهَا مِنْهُ وَأَدْخَلَ بِهَا عَلَى سَيِّدَتِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Qamara al-Zamāni jaʿala khātama al-sitti Budūra fī ṭayyi al-waraqati wa-nāwalahā li-al-khādimi fa-akhadhahā minhu wa-adkhala bihā ʿalā sayyidatihi
sentences.l: Then indeed Qamar al-Zamān put (the) ring (of) the-Lady Budūr in (the) fold (of) the-sheet and-handed-it to-the-eunuch, and-he-took-it from-him and-brought-in with-it to his-lady.
sentences.i: Then Qamar al-Zamān put the Lady Budūr's ring in the fold of the paper and handed it to the eunuch, who took it from him and carried it in to his mistress.
sentences.n: jaʿala fī, “to put in”. ṭayy, “fold”, the verbal noun of ṭawā, “to fold”; its shadda is printed. The print spells fī as فى, with ى. nāwala, Form III, “to hand”; li- marks the one handed to, where Classical usage puts him as a second object. adkhala bihā ʿalā, “he brought it in to”: adkhala, Form IV, already means “to bring in”, and the bi- of dakhala bi-, “to go in with”, is added as well, a doubling found in later Arabic; ʿalā marks the person visited. al-sitt, the later word for “lady”.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. The rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥ / al-mubāḥ.
